claim_text: Controllers should not transmit to an aircraft during take-off, initial climb, the last part of final approach or the landing roll, unless it is necessary for safety reasons.
Phraseology for initiating engine start includes: 'READY TO START UP', 'START NUMBER ONE', or 'STARTING NUMBER ONE'.
Phraseology for approving start up includes: '[Callsign] START UP APPROVED [QNH]'.
Phraseology for approving start up at a specific time includes: '[Callsign] START UP AT [Time] [QNH]'.
Having received ATC approval, the pilot starts the engines assisted as necessary by ground crew.
Phraseology for indicating expected departure time with start up at own discretion includes: '[Callsign] EXPECT DEPARTURE AT [Time] START UP AT OWN DISCRETION [QNH]'.
Where no ATIS is provided, the pilot may ask for current aerodrome information before requesting start up.
Phraseology for indicating expected start up time includes: '[Callsign] EXPECT START UP AT [Time] [QNH]'.
Along with the request to start engines, the pilot will state the location of the aircraft and acknowledge receipt of the ATIS broadcast.
When the departure of the aircraft will be delayed, the controller will normally indicate a start up time or an expected start up time.
When the traffic circuit is in a right-hand pattern, this should be specified.
Requests for instructions to join the traffic circuit should be made in sufficient time to allow for a planned entry into the circuit taking other traffic into account.
Where ATIS is provided, receipt of the broadcast should be acknowledged in the initial call to the aerodrome.
Depending on prevailing traffic conditions and the direction from which an aircraft is arriving, it may be possible to give a straight-in-approach.

Pilot entering the circuit shall provide position reports in accordance with local procedures.
At aerodromes equipped with ATIS, the pilot should confirm having listened to the ATIS message when establishing contact with the tower.
Depending on traffic situation and arrival direction, a straight-in approach may be possible.
The pilot, having joined the traffic circuit, shall make routine reports as required by local procedures.
When a vehicle is moving on the movement area it may be necessary to inform the vehicle of a potentially dangerous situation and to instruct it to stop.
Under no circumstances shall a driver cross a runway unless positive permission has been given and acknowledged.
Drivers of vehicles required to tow aircraft should not assume that the receiving station is aware that an aircraft is to be towed.
If a vehicle is operating on the runway, it shall be instructed to leave the runway when it is expected that an aircraft will be landing or taking off.
Drivers should state the type, and where applicable the operator, of the aircraft to be towed.
A runway vacated report shall not be made until the vehicle (and tow) is clear of the designated runway area, beyond the holding point.
When vehicles are operating in close proximity to aircraft, drivers should be extremely vigilant and comply in full with local procedures and ATC instructions.
When the controller replies 'HOLD POSITION', the driver shall not proceed until the controller calls back with permission.
Permission to proceed on the apron may include instructions regarding other traffic necessary to ensure safe operations.
Drivers on first-call should identify themselves by their vehicle call sign, state their position and intended destination and, when possible, the required route.
If the defined point is not the intended destination, drivers must stop at this point and request permission before proceeding further.
When a controller replies 'standby', the driver shall not proceed until permission is given.
Phraseology for air-taxi to helicopter stand involves controller instruction 'AIR-TAXI TO HELICOPTER STAND' and pilot readback 'AIR-TAXI TO HELICOPTER STAND, [Callsign]'.
Pilots should remain on tower frequency until the runway is vacated, unless otherwise advised.
Controllers should not give taxi instructions to pilots until the landing roll is completed, unless absolutely necessary.
Phraseology for vacating runway and taxiing involves controller instruction 'TAKE FIRST RIGHT WHEN VACATED' followed by frequency change, and pilot readback 'FIRST RIGHT, [Frequency] [Callsign]'.
Phraseology for contacting ground control after vacating involves pilot stating 'RUNWAY VACATED' and controller issuing taxi instructions 'TAXI TO [Stand] VIA [Taxiway]'.
If there is doubt that a message has been correctly received, a repetition of the messages shall be requested either in full or in part.
When an aircraft wishes to broadcast information to aircraft in its vicinity, the message should be prefaced by the call "ALL STATIONS".
No reply is expected to such general calls unless individual stations are subsequently called upon to acknowledge receipt.
When establishing communications, an aircraft should use the full call sign of both the aircraft and the aeronautical station.
When a ground station wishes to broadcast information, the message should be prefaced by the call "ALL STATIONS".
During this procedure, the aircraft shall also advise the time of its next intended transmission.

When an aeronautical station has been unable to establish contact with an aircraft after calls on the frequencies on which the aircraft is believed to be listening, it shall request other aeronautical stations to render assistance by calling the aircraft and relaying traffic, if necessary.

If the attempts specified in 9.5.6 fail, the aeronautical station should transmit messages addressed to the aircraft, other than messages containing air traffic control clearances, by blind transmission on the frequency(ies) on which the aircraft is believed to be listening.

When an aircraft is unable to establish communication due to receiver failure, it shall transmit reports at the scheduled times, or positions, on the frequency in use, preceded by the phrase "TRANSMITTING BLIND DUE RECEIVER FAILURE".

An aircraft which is provided with air traffic control or advisory service shall, in addition to complying with 9.5.3, transmit information regarding the intention of the pilot-in-command with respect to the continuation of the flight of the aircraft.
When an aircraft is unable to establish communication due to airborne equipment failure, it shall, if so equipped, select the appropriate SSR code to indicate radio failure (7600).
The aircraft shall transmit the intended message, following this by a complete repetition.
When transmitting blind, the aircraft may include the addressee(s) for which the message is intended if necessary.
Blind transmission of air traffic control clearances shall not be made to aircraft, except at the specific request of the originator.

When an aeronautical station has been unable to establish contact with an aircraft after calls on the frequencies on which the aircraft is believed to be listening, it shall request aircraft on the route to attempt to establish communication with the aircraft and relay messages, if necessary.
If the attempts specified under 9.5.1 fail, the aircraft shall transmit its message twice on the designated frequency(ies), preceded by the phrase "TRANSMITTING BLIND".
General rules that are applicable in the event of communications failure are contained in Annex 10,Volume II.
When an aircraft station fails to establish contact with the aeronautical station on the designated frequency, it shall attempt to establish contact on another frequency appropriate to the route.
If this attempt fails, the aircraft shall attempt to establish communication with other aircraft or other aeronautical stations on frequencies appropriate to the route.

A distress message should contain as many as possible of the following elements, and, if possible, in the order shown: name of the station addressed, identification of the aircraft, nature of the distress condition, intention of the person in command, position, level and heading of the aircraft, and any other useful information.
The station addressed in a distress message will normally be the station communicating with the aircraft or the station in whose area of responsibility the aircraft is operating.

Aircraft in distress may use any means at their disposal to attract attention and make known their condition, including the activation of SSR code 7700. Stations may use any means to assist an aircraft in distress.
Variation on the elements listed under 9.2.1.1 is permissible when the transmitting station is not itself in distress, provided that such a circumstance is clearly stated.
When the ground station controlling the distress traffic is aware that the aircraft is no longer in distress, it shall terminate the distress communication and silence condition.
An aircraft in distress or a station in control of distress traffic may impose silence, either on all aircraft on the frequency or on a particular aircraft which interferes with the distress traffic.
Aircraft requested to maintain radio silence shall maintain it until advised that the distress traffic has ended.
A distress message should contain elements in the order shown in section 9.2.1.1 if possible.
Superfluous transmissions may be distracting at a time when the pilot's hands are already full.
Pilots making distress or urgency calls should attempt to speak slowly and distinctly so as to avoid any unnecessary repetition.
Urgency messages have priority over all transmissions except distress messages.
Distress communications should be continued on the current frequency until it is considered that better assistance can be provided by changing to another frequency.
Provisions are not intended to prevent the use of any other communications frequency if considered necessary or desirable, including maritime mobile service RTF calling frequencies.
Distress messages have priority over all other transmissions.

Aeronautical stations shall refrain from further use of a frequency on which distress or urgency traffic is heard, unless directly involved in rendering assistance or until after the emergency traffic has been terminated.
A station replying (or originating a reply) to an aircraft in distress or urgency should provide such advice, information and instructions as is necessary to assist the pilot.
Pilots should seek assistance whenever there is any doubt as to the safety of a flight.
Distress is defined as a condition of being threatened by serious and/or imminent danger and of requiring immediate assistance.

When a distress message has been intercepted which apparently receives no acknowledgement, the aircraft intercepting the distress message should, if time and circumstances seem appropriate, acknowledge the message and then broadcast it.
Pilots should adapt the phraseology procedures in this chapter to their specific needs and to the time available.
If the ground station called by the aircraft in distress or urgency does not reply, then any other ground station or aircraft shall reply and give whatever assistance possible.
The words MAYDAY or PAN PAN, as appropriate, should preferably be spoken three times at the start of the initial distress or urgency call.
Distress and urgency communication procedures are detailed in Annex 10, Volume II.
Urgency is defined as a condition concerning the safety of an aircraft or other vehicle, or of some person on board or within sight, but which does not require immediate assistance.
A distress or urgency call should normally be made on the frequency in use at the time.
The word MAYDAY spoken at the start identifies a distress message, and the words PAN PAN spoken at the start identifies an urgency message.
Essential aerodrome information includes information regarding water on a runway, a taxiway or an apron.
Essential aerodrome information may be omitted when it is known that the aircraft has received all or part of the information from other sources.
Essential aerodrome information is information regarding the movement area and its associated facilities which is necessary to ensure the safe operation of aircraft.
Essential aerodrome information should be passed to aircraft whenever possible prior to start-up or taxi and prior to the commencement of final approach.
Essential aerodrome information includes information regarding rough or broken surfaces on a runway, a taxiway or an apron, whether marked or not.
Essential aerodrome information includes information regarding construction or maintenance work on, or immediately adjacent to the movement area.
Essential aerodrome information includes information regarding snow banks or drifts adjacent to a runway, a taxiway or an apron.
Example phraseology for essential aerodrome information includes CAUTION messages for construction work and reports on lighting serviceability, hazards, and runway conditions.
Essential aerodrome information includes information regarding other temporary hazards, including parked aircraft and birds on the ground or in the air.
Essential aerodrome information includes information regarding failure or irregular operation of part or all of the aerodrome lighting systems.
Essential aerodrome information includes information regarding snow, slush or ice on a runway, a taxiway or an apron.
Essential aerodrome information includes information regarding any other pertinent information.
A 'FINAL' report shall be made when an aircraft turns onto final within 7 km (4 NM) from touchdown, or at 7 km (4 NM) if no landing clearance was received at the 'LONG FINAL' point.
Pilots may request to carry out a 'TOUCH AND GO' to save taxiing time when training in the traffic circuit.
When describing undercarriage condition during a low pass, the phrase 'WHEELS APPEAR UP' may be used.
When describing undercarriage condition during a low pass, the phrase 'LANDING GEAR APPEARS DOWN' may be used.
When describing undercarriage condition during a low pass, the phrase 'RIGHT (or LEFT, or NOSE) WHEEL DOES NOT APPEAR UP (or DOWN)' may be used.
A 'LONG FINAL' report shall be made when an aircraft turns onto final at a distance greater than 7 km (4 NM) from touchdown.
A pilot may request to fly past the control tower or other observation point for the purpose of visual inspection from the ground.
For a straight-in approach, a 'LONG FINAL' report shall be made at about 15 km (8 NM) from touchdown.
When describing undercarriage condition during a low pass, the phrase 'RIGHT (or LEFT, or NOSE) WHEEL APPEARS UP (or DOWN)' may be used.
ATC may clear an aircraft for a 'TOUCH AND GO' using the phrase 'CLEARED TOUCH AND GO'.
Example dialogue illustrates the exchange for a low pass request and clearance.
If unable to approve a 'TOUCH AND GO' due to traffic, ATC may instruct the pilot to 'MAKE FULL STOP' or 'MAKE ANOTHER CIRCUIT REPORT DOWNWIND'.
For training purposes, a pilot may request permission to make an approach along, or parallel to, the runway, without landing.
Example dialogue illustrates the exchange for 'LONG FINAL' and 'FINAL' reports including wind and landing clearance.
Unless instructions are issued to the contrary, an aircraft on an instrument approach will carry out the missed approach procedure.
Any transmissions to aircraft going around should be brief and kept to a minimum.
Unless instructions are issued to the contrary, an aircraft operating VFR will continue in the normal traffic circuit.
Power-back is used by aircraft to reverse using the power of their engines (e.g. turboprop aircraft).
Requests for push-back or power-back are made to ATC or apron management depending on the local procedures.
When the manoeuvre is complete the ground crew gives the pilot a visual signal to indicate that the aircraft is free to taxi.
Should the pilot wish to stop the manoeuvre at any stage, the phrase 'stop push-back' should be used.
The phraseology listed in section 4.3.2 should be used by the pilot and the ground crew to coordinate the push-back.
Clearances and instructions to enter, land on, take off from, hold short of, cross and backtrack on any runway shall always be read back.
Runway-in-use, altimeter settings, SSR codes, level instructions, heading and speed instructions, and transition levels shall always be read back.
Whenever possible, controllers should pass a route clearance to an aircraft before start-up.
Other clearances or instructions, including conditional clearances, shall be read back or acknowledged in a manner to clearly indicate that they have been understood and will be complied with.
ATC route clearances shall always be read back.

Controllers should pass a clearance slowly and clearly, avoid passing clearances during complicated taxiing, and on no occasion should a clearance be passed when the pilot is engaged in line up or take-off manoeuvres.
The words 'TAKE OFF' are used only when an aircraft is cleared for take-off, or when canceling a take-off clearance; at other times, the word 'DEPARTURE' or 'AIRBORNE' is used.
An ATC route clearance is not an instruction to take off or enter an active runway.
The controller shall listen to the read-back to ascertain that the clearance or instruction has been correctly acknowledged by the flight crew.
An aircraft should terminate the read-back by its call sign.
The controller shall take immediate action to correct any discrepancies revealed by the read-back.
See: APPENDIX 1 DIFFERENCES FROM ICAO RADIOTELEPHONY PROCEDURES
Phraseology 'RUNWAY [designator] CLEARED FOR TAKE-OFF' is used after line-up for immediate departure.
Phraseology 'LINE UP. BE READY FOR IMMEDIATE DEPARTURE' is used to instruct line-up with readiness for immediate departure.
At busy aerodromes with separate GROUND and TOWER functions, aircraft are usually transferred to the TOWER at, or when approaching, the runway-holding position.
Phraseology 'ARE YOU READY FOR IMMEDIATE DEPARTURE' is used to query readiness for immediate departure.
Except in cases of emergency, controllers should not transmit to an aircraft in the process of taking off or during the early stage of climb.
Phraseology 'LINE UP AND WAIT' is used for line-up instructions, acknowledged by 'LINING UP [callsign]'.
Care should be taken to ensure that the phraseology employed during taxi manoeuvres cannot be interpreted as a clearance to enter the runway or to take-off.
When a conditional clearance involves a departing aircraft and an arriving aircraft, the departing aircraft must correctly identify the arriving aircraft on which the clearance is based.
Conditional clearances shall not be used for movements affecting the active runway(s), except when the aircraft or vehicles concerned are seen by both the controller and pilot.
A conditional clearance shall be given as follows: 1) call sign; 2) the condition; 3) the clearance; 4) brief reiteration of the condition.
Reference to the arriving aircraft type may be insufficient for conditional clearances; it may be necessary to add a description of the colour or the company name to ensure correct identification.
In poor visibility, the controller may request the pilot to report when airborne.
When a pilot abandons the take-off manoeuvre, the control tower should be so informed as soon as practicable.
When a pilot abandons the take-off manoeuvre, assistance or taxi instructions should be requested as required.
Departure instructions may be given with the take-off clearance to ensure separation between aircraft operating in the vicinity of the aerodrome.

When an aircraft has commenced the take-off roll and it is necessary to abandon take-off to avert a dangerous traffic situation, the aircraft should be instructed to stop immediately and the instruction and call sign repeated.
It is occasionally necessary to cancel the take-off clearance due to unexpected traffic developments or a departing aircraft taking longer than anticipated.
It is occasionally necessary to quickly free the runway for landing traffic due to unexpected traffic developments or a departing aircraft taking longer than anticipated.
When several runways are in use and there is any possibility that the pilot may be confused as to which one to use, the runway number should be stated in the take-off clearance.
The clearance limit for departing aircraft may be any other position on the aerodrome depending on prevailing traffic circumstances.
When a taxi clearance contains a taxi limit beyond a runway, it shall contain an explicit clearance to cross, or an instruction to hold short of that runway.
For departing aircraft, the clearance limit will normally be the taxi-holding point of the runway in use.
Where an aircraft acknowledges receipt of the ATIS broadcast, the controller does not need to pass departure information to the pilot when giving taxiing instructions.
A taxi instruction issued by a controller must always contain a clearance limit, which is the point at which the aircraft must stop until further permission to proceed is given.
The runway is considered vacated when the entire aircraft is beyond the relevant runway-holding position.
Test transmissions should include the identification of the aeronautical station being called, the aircraft identification, the words "RADIO CHECK", and the frequency being used.
When a pilot receives an instruction or clearance they cannot execute, they should notify using the words 'NIE MOGĘ' and provide the reason.
Replies to test transmissions should include the identification of the station calling, the identification of the station replying, and information regarding the readability of the transmission.
Ground station test signals for transmitter or receiver adjustment shall not continue for more than 10 seconds and shall be composed of spoken numbers followed by the radio call sign of the station.
The readability of transmissions should be classified using the scale: 1. Unreadable, 2. Readable now and then, 3. Readable but with difficulty, 4. Readable, 5. Perfectly readable.
An aircraft shall be advised by the appropriate aeronautical station to change from one radio frequency to another in accordance with agreed procedures.
Phraseology for frequency change includes 'CONTACT [Unit] [Frequency]' and readback 'Frequency Callsign'.
In the absence of such advice, the aircraft shall notify the aeronautical station before such a change takes place.
When an aircraft announces that it is making an emergency descent, the controller will take all possible action to safeguard other aircraft.
An urgency message should contain as many of the elements detailed in 9.2.1.1 as are required by the circumstances.
All other stations should take care not to interfere with the transmission of urgency traffic.

The call should be made on the frequency in use at the time, and the station addressed will normally be that station communicating with the aircraft, or the station in whose area of responsibility the aircraft is operating.
The general broadcast to warn aircraft of an emergency descent should be followed, as necessary, by specific instructions.
Further questions might be asked of the pilot in order to assist in ascertaining the position of the aircraft.
